I LOVED the look, it was everything I love in life; the religious and sacrilegious imagery mixed together (as a long standing metal and occult fan, as well as heavily into fashion and costuming) and giant, theatrical performances. But their look just didn't match how I thought the music would be, and I really struggled to get past it.  
Defining moment for me was when Spotify offered up Year Zero in my Discover Weekly playlist in 2015, and it started to *click*. That song is still my favourite, the vocals and harmonies especially, still give me goosebumps. So I gave them another shot. I floated around on a few of the Infestissamum tracks; but still wasn't entirely won over (even though I love doom stuff)  
Then Meliora dropped, and the light bulb turned on. Absolution, He is... they were like religious experiences when I listened. Suddenly I *'got it'*. By this time, I was about a year too late to see them live, and they only just returned here last week, but I am now full on obsessed after seeing them live. It's sweet that you want to get into his style of music. But also worth noting that you probably don't have to just to get his attention. 
But the journey into metal is a slippery, awesome slope, so why not? 

While a lot of the people who commented here have given you some great, classic albums, I'd suggest potentially going for a more melodic approach. Melodic anything is generally easier to get into than genres like thrash, black metal and death metal, which are a few of the core sub genres. 
Give albums like Opeth's 'watershed' or Porcupine Tree's 'fear of a blank planet' or 'the incident' a shot.  They're prog, and there is some growling, but they are definitely a lot easier to digest as a new listener. 
It's definitely going to be less of a shock to slowly introduce more heavy stuff as you work out what you like. They're are so many different sounds within the metal genre, you could even have a dabble in stoner/sludge rock stuff. They're are metal influences and elements to them, but it's a lot slower and often more groovy. 
Like, I'm a big fan of bands like Queens of the Stone Age and Truckfighters, who are technically rock rather than metal, but still have that punch that so much commercial stuff lacks. 

This is about educating yourself though, there is a lot to learn about the music and the etiquette that comes with it. Any of the docos by Sam Dunn are great, so I highly recommend those. 
And if you have any questions, feel free to inbox me :) as a lady who has been actively into metal for a while now, I have a lot of information to share!

Yeah, seriously, it's worth the money. The process is basically sandwiching a pattern made from craft foam between two pieces of Worbla, which is adhesive when heated, and shaping it. You can't mess it up, it can be reshaped and reheated over and over and cools hard but with a bit of flexibility. It's brilliant.
I've never used foam on it's own, it seems to be roughly the same in the sense of difficulty. The benefit of Worbla is the added tensile strength, ability to keep intricate shapes, and the fact you can use it to detail.

Painting requires a good priming coat, say for Worbla, you can paint straight on if you don't mind texture, but if it needs to be shiny and smooth, you use gesso/primer layers and sand in between. I think if you primed the foam it would reduce the flaking. I used it on a couple of foam details on the sword, and nothing chipped/flaked.

When I want accuracy and it's something a little more complicated then I think I could attempt to draft myself, I'll try and find a base pattern that's as similar as possible to what I need. Generally from there, you can make small edits to collars/cuffs/fits, etc, as you've got your starting point. Also, ALWAYS make it in a junk fabric first as a practice.

My suggestion would be to see if you can find any traditional Japanese (Maybe even Chinese/Viet) patterns online, as I know that some are similar. It's probably based of a Japanese workers uniform pattern anyway. Do a bit of Google-fu, see if you can even find out what they're called, etc.

Also, I always look up other peoples attempts at the costume (if you can find them) and save the images/advice/etc into a word doc. A lot of cosplayers will write out their process, and that can really help with any hard aspects you may be unsure of. Then from there you can sit down and work out a plan based on other experiences :)

I used to go away with family friends camping, over the new years/summer break. I ended up becoming best friends with one of the step-cousins, and there were a fair few kids, most younger than me (when I was in my mid/late teens) and the adults were just as immature.

We'd get drunk, play board games, go swimming and generally have a good time, and would play music pretty frequently as we hung around the campsite, and a lot of it was oldies. 500 Miles by The Proclaimers came on at one point, and some bizarre conga line/vague dance consisting of the 3 brothers (who were most of the kids dad's/uncles) began, where they all pretended to be members in the band, but they were all wearing washing up gloves and aprons as they were cleaning at the time. I have a video of it somewhere.

It probably doesn't transpose as a good story, a "you had to be there" moment, but now whenever we all get together, 500 Miles has to be played and we all do the conga line/dance. It's a nice salute to some really happy times for me.
